prompt.context: Copier Co. is a national distributor of office equipment, particularly commercial-grade copiers. The firm sells the equipment directly to companies for use in their offices, as well as provides regular service including maintenance, repairs, and replacing disposable parts. Recently, the company has experienced declining profit margins.
prompt.question: We have been hired to determine why profit margins are declining and what to do to reverse the trend.

clarifying_info.q: How does the sales process work?
clarifying_info.a: The company bids on contracts; contracts are typically awarded to the lowest bidder. The bid consists of a per-copier cost which includes 1 year of maintenance as part of the sales price. Salespeople have free rein to determine bid price and are compensated based on commission (percentage of overall sales).

There is one major competitor (American Copiers) and a new low-cost competitor (Bottom Dollar Copier) that has recently entered the market. All three companies are distributors and service technicians, NOT manufacturers.
This case focuses on one identical copier sold and distributed by multiple firms.

exhibits.title: Bid Price vs. Number of Copiers in Contract
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot showing individual contract data points, with the number of copiers in the contract on the x-axis and the per-copier bid price on the y-axis.
exhibits.data: X-axis: number of copiers per contract (ranges roughly 5 to 50+). Y-axis: bid price per copier (ranges roughly $2,000 to $7,000+). Data points are scattered across the chart; most are concentrated at lower copier counts with higher bid prices, with a cluster of points at higher copier counts at lower bid prices. A few outlier points show high bid prices at higher copier counts.

exhibits.title: Copier Co. Successful Bid Info
exhibits.shows: A table comparing three competitive scenarios: competing against American Copier only, competing against Bottom Dollar Copier only, and competing against both AC and BDC. Rows show average bid price, average copiers in order, cost of copier, service cost per page printed, and average pages printed per copier per month.
exhibits.data: Competing vs AC only: avg bid price $5,000, avg copiers 20, copier cost $3,000, service cost $0.05/page, avg pages/copier/month 1,000. Competing vs BDC only: avg bid price $4,000, avg copiers 25, copier cost $3,000, service cost $0.05/page, avg pages/copier/month 1,000. Competing vs both AC and BDC: avg bid price $3,000, avg copiers 30, copier cost $3,000, service cost $0.05/page, avg pages/copier/month 1,000.

framework: Revenue drivers: volume (number of contracts/copiers sold) and price (average bid price per copier)
Cost drivers: fixed costs (sales force base, warehousing, overhead) and variable costs (service/labor, COGS, transportation, sales commission)

Non-financial factors: competition (size and share of AC and BDC, bidding process dynamics), product (quality and characteristics), customer (changing preferences, different market segments), company (salesforce compensation structure, product mix)

questions.prompt: Show Exhibit 1 (bid price vs. number of copiers). What do you observe and what hypotheses does this raise?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify a negative correlation — larger contracts (more copiers) are associated with lower per-copier bid prices. Good response: hypothesize that salespeople are lowering bid prices on large contracts to win higher total commission (more copiers x lower price still yields higher total sales). Great response: note the few high-bid outliers at high copier counts and ask for competitive breakdown of bid prices to understand if competitor presence drives price down.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate profit per copier and total profit for bids competing against American Copier only.
questions.guidance: Candidate must remember service is 1 year (12 months) and pages are given per month. Common pitfall: forgetting to annualize pages printed. Work on a contribution basis (bid price minus copier cost minus annual service cost).

math.setup: Profit per copier = Bid price - Copier cost - Annual service cost. Annual service cost = pages/month x 12 months x cost/page = 1,000 x 12 x $0.05 = $600. Contribution per copier = $5,000 - $3,000 = $2,000. Profit per copier = $2,000 - $600 = $1,400. Total profit = $1,400 x 20 copiers = $28,000.
steps: Annual service cost = 1,000 pages/month x 12 months x $0.05/page = $600
math.answer: $1,400 profit per copier; $28,000 total profit per contract

questions.prompt: Are bids competing against Bottom Dollar Copier only, or against both competitors, profitable?
questions.guidance: Candidate should reason through quickly without full long-form math. Good response: vs BDC only is profitable but less so ($400/copier, $10,000 total). Vs both competitors, contribution per copier is $0 ($3,000 bid - $3,000 cost), so after service costs the contract loses $600 per copier ($18,000 total loss). Candidate should conclude that competing in three-way bids is value-destroying.

math.setup: Same formula. Vs BDC only: contribution = $4,000 - $3,000 = $1,000; profit/copier = $1,000 - $600 = $400; total = $400 x 25 = $10,000. Vs both: contribution = $3,000 - $3,000 = $0; profit/copier = $0 - $600 = -$600; total = -$600 x 30 = -$18,000.
steps: Vs BDC only: contribution = $4,000 - $3,000 = $1,000; profit/copier = $1,000 - $600 = $400; total profit = $400 x 25 = $10,000
Vs both AC and BDC: contribution = $3,000 - $3,000 = $0; profit/copier = $0 - $600 = -$600; total profit = -$600 x 30 = -$18,000
math.answer: Vs BDC only: $10,000 profit per contract. Vs both competitors: -$18,000 loss per contract.

brainstorming.prompt: Management wants to continue bidding on all contracts, including three-way competitive bids. What solutions can you suggest to address the profitability problem in low-margin or loss-making bidding scenarios?

categories.name: Pricing controls
ideas: Set minimum allowable bid prices for salespeople to prevent undercutting
Require management approval for bids below a profitability threshold

categories.name: Compensation restructuring
ideas: Change compensation from commission on total sales to commission on profit or margin
Align incentives so salespeople are rewarded for profitable bids, not just volume

categories.name: Product and service packaging
ideas: Offer a no-service-component package at a lower bid price to reduce cost base
Offer multi-year service contracts to generate recurring revenue and improve lifetime value
Bundle complementary products (paper, other office equipment) to increase contract value

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Negotiate better pricing with copier manufacturers to lower COGS
Optimize service delivery to reduce per-page service cost

categories.name: Strategic partnerships
ideas: Explore joint ventures or teaming agreements with competitors on large orders to share costs and avoid destructive price wars

recommendation: The primary driver of declining margins is the entry of Bottom Dollar Copier, which has intensified price competition, particularly in three-way bids where Copier Co. bids at or below its cost of goods. This is compounded by a commission structure that incentivizes salespeople to lower bid prices on large contracts to maximize total sales volume.
Immediate action: implement minimum bid price floors to eliminate loss-making three-way bids, and restructure sales compensation to reward margin rather than revenue.
risks: Minimum bid floors may cause Copier Co. to lose large contracts to BDC in the short term, reducing volume.
Changing compensation may cause salesforce attrition or resistance.
BDC may continue to undercut on price, making three-way bids structurally unprofitable regardless of internal policy.
next_steps: Analyze the proportion of total contracts that are three-way bids to quantify total profit impact.
Model the financial impact of revised compensation structures and minimum bid floors.
Assess whether BDC's pricing is sustainable long-term (predatory pricing vs. lower cost structure).
Explore product differentiation or service enhancements to justify premium pricing over BDC.
